title: Debt Consolidation Loan vs Balance Transfer: Real Costs
description: Debt consolidation loan vs balance transfer card: the same $6,000 paid three ways, what each really costs, and options if your credit is fair.

takeaways: A 0% balance transfer is usually cheapest, if you clear the balance before the promo ends.
A consolidation loan costs more but gives a fixed, smaller payment and an end date.
Neither fixes the spending. Run the numbers in the free comparison sheet before you apply.
body:
If you owe money on a credit card, you have probably seen both offers. A new card promises 0% interest for a year or more if you move your balance over. A lender offers one loan that pays off your cards and replaces them with a single monthly payment. Both sound cheaper than the rate you are paying now, and both can be. Both can also end up costing you more than doing nothing fancy at all. Most comparisons list features side by side and stop there. This one runs the money instead. Below, the same $6,000 credit card debt gets paid three ways, with the math done in full. After that comes a section most guides skip: what to do if your credit is only fair, because the best 0% offers are usually not aimed at you. ## The short answer If you qualify for a 0% transfer and you can clear the balance before the promotional period ends, the transfer is usually the cheapest option by a wide margin. In the worked example below, it costs $240 in total. The consolidation loan costs more, about $1,174 in interest, but the monthly payment is smaller, the end date is fixed from day one, and there is no deadline cliff. Staying on the card costs the most here: roughly $1,739 in interest, even paying a solid $300 a month. The real question is not which product is best. It is which plan you will actually finish. A cheap plan abandoned in month four costs more than a pricier one you stick with. ## How each option works ### The balance transfer card A balance transfer moves debt from your current card onto a new card, usually at 0% interest for a set promotional window. According to Experian, those introductory periods typically run from 12 to 21 months. The transfer is not free. You pay a balance transfer fee, usually 3% to 5% of the amount you move, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) notes the fee is either a percentage of the transfer or a fixed amount, whichever is more, and it gets added to your new balance. When the window closes, whatever is left starts accruing interest at the card's standard rate, which Experian says can reach nearly 30%. Two more traps are worth knowing. The CFPB warns that new purchases on the same card lose their grace period, so they collect interest until everything is paid off. And if you are ever more than 60 days late, the issuer can raise your rate on all balances, including the transferred one. You also may not be able to move the whole debt: the new card's transfer limit can be lower than what you owe, leaving part of the balance behind at the old rate. ### The debt consolidation loan A consolidation loan is a personal loan from a bank, credit union, or online lender. The lender pays off your cards, and you repay the loan in fixed monthly payments over a set term. Your rate depends mostly on your credit, and some lenders add an origination fee on top. As Experian points out, the rate has to be low enough for the loan to save you money at all, which sounds obvious and still gets ignored constantly. The CFPB adds two cautions. Some low advertised rates are teaser rates that rise later. And a smaller monthly payment is not always a win: it often just means a longer repayment period, so you pay more in total. That is why every comparison below uses total cost, not the monthly figure. ## The same $6,000 of debt, paid three ways Here is the worked example. These numbers are an illustration with made-up rates, not a quote from any lender. Say you owe $6,000 on one card at 24% APR. That is higher than average but not unusual: the Federal Reserve put the average card APR at about 21% as of May 2026, and plenty of cards sit above that. You can afford roughly $300 a month toward the debt. ### Option 1: Stay on the card Pay $300 a month at 24% APR and the debt is gone in 26 months. You pay about $1,739 in interest along the way, so the $6,000 debt costs you $7,739 in total. That assumes a steady $300 every month. Drop to minimum payments and the timeline stretches out for years, with far more interest. ### Option 2: Move it to a 0% balance transfer Now say you qualify for a card offering 0% for 18 months with a 4% transfer fee, in the middle of the usual 3% to 5% range. The fee on $6,000 is $240, so your new balance is $6,240 and the clock starts. To clear it before the promo ends, you need to pay $6,240 divided by 18, which is about $347 a month. Pay that, and your total cost is the $240 fee. No interest at all. That is roughly $1,499 cheaper than staying on the card, and you are done eight months sooner. Now the honest catch. That $347 is more than the $300 you were paying before. If you transfer the balance and keep paying $250 a month out of habit, you will still owe $1,740 when the promo ends. At that point the rate jumps, say to 26% in this illustration, and paying $250 a month takes eight more months and about $167 more in interest. Your total cost is about $407, still less than staying on the card, but it took 26 months and left no room for a single bad month. The transfer rewards one specific behavior: paying the higher amount, every month, without fail. ### Option 3: Take a consolidation loan Finally, say a lender offers you $6,000 at 12% APR fixed over 36 months, with no origination fee in this example. Your payment is about $199 a month. Over the three years you pay about $1,174 in interest, for a total of $7,174. That is about $565 cheaper than staying on the card, and about $934 more than a transfer handled perfectly. In exchange, you get the lowest monthly payment of the three, a rate that cannot jump, and a payoff date that is fixed the day you sign. TABLE: | | Stay on the card | Balance transfer | Consolidation loan | |------------------------|----------------------|----------------------------|------------------------| | Rate | 24% APR | 0% for 18 months, then 26% | 12% fixed | | Upfront fee | None | $240 (4% of balance) | None in this example | | Monthly payment | $300 | $347 to clear it in time | $199 | | Months to debt-free | 26 | 18 | 36 | | Interest and fees paid | $1,739 | $240 | $1,174 | | Total paid overall | $7,739 | $6,240 | $7,174 | Your balance, rate, and offers will be different, so run your own version of this table before you apply for anything. No sign-up needed. ![The comparison table showing monthly payment, interest and fees, and total paid for staying on the card, a balance transfer and a loan](/assets/img/posts/debt-consolidation-comparison-preview-1180x332.webp) ## So which one should you pick? Pick the balance transfer if your credit score is around 670 or higher, the debt is small enough to clear inside the promo window, and the required monthly payment genuinely fits your budget. Pick the loan if the debt is bigger, you need longer than 18 to 21 months, or you know a fixed payment and a fixed end date will keep you on track better than a deadline will. Pick neither, and just attack the card directly, if the fees and rates on offer would leave you no better off. Our guide on [how to pay off credit card debt fast](/blog/pay-off-credit-card-debt-fast/) walks through that direct approach step by step. One thing neither product does is fix the spending that built the balance. If the card creeps back up after you consolidate, you end up with the loan and a fresh card balance, which is worse than where you started. If your budget keeps springing leaks, [why your budget keeps failing](/blog/why-your-budget-keeps-failing/) is worth a read before you sign anything. ## What if your credit is only fair? Plenty of guides quietly assume a strong credit score. If yours sits in the low 600s, here is the version of this advice that actually applies to you. First, the 0% route is probably closed, and it is better to know that now. Experian notes that balance transfer cards are not usually an option for applicants with poor or fair credit, and the strongest offers generally go to people with scores of at least 670. Apply anyway and you may pick up a hard inquiry, which can trim a few points off your score, in exchange for a decline or a credit limit too small to move your balance. Second, a consolidation loan will be easier to get, but check the rate with clear eyes. At 18% APR over 36 months, the same $6,000 loan costs about $1,809 in interest. That is more than the $1,739 you would pay by staying on the card and paying $300 a month. A loan with a rate close to your card's rate is not a rescue. It is the same debt wearing a different outfit, sometimes with an origination fee added. Third, you still have real options. Ask your current card issuer for a lower rate or a hardship arrangement; the CFPB suggests contacting creditors directly, since some will agree to lower payments or reduce a rate to help you pay the debt back. Ask a local credit union what it can offer, since credit unions sometimes approve smaller loans that big lenders turn away. Talk to a nonprofit credit counselor about a debt management plan, where the agency negotiates lower rates with your creditors and you make one monthly payment; the CFPB points people to nonprofit counselors for free support. Or skip new credit altogether and pay the card down with the [debt snowball vs avalanche](/blog/debt-snowball-vs-avalanche/) methods while you rebuild your score, which [how to build credit from scratch](/blog/how-to-build-credit-from-scratch/) covers from the ground up. One warning that matters. The CFPB flags companies that charge upfront fees to settle your debts for less, or that tell you to stop paying your bills and send them the money instead. That path usually wrecks your credit and can leave you owing more than when you started. A legitimate nonprofit counselor will not ask for big fees upfront. ## Before you sign anything - Work out the total cost of each option, fees included, not just the monthly payment. - For a transfer, divide the new balance by the number of promo months. That figure is your real monthly payment, whatever the minimum says. - Set up an automatic payment for the day after payday, so a busy month cannot sink the plan. - Do not use the balance transfer card for purchases. You lose the grace period and muddy the payoff math. - Keep paying your old card until the transfer shows as complete, so you avoid a late fee in between. - Decide what happens to the old card once it is empty, and review the whole picture monthly; [the 20-minute monthly money review](/blog/monthly-money-review/) shows a simple way to do it in half an hour. ## Frequently asked questions ### Which is cheaper, a balance transfer or a consolidation loan? Usually the transfer, if you finish inside the promo window. In the $6,000 example above, the transfer cost $240, the loan cost $1,174 in interest, and staying on the card cost $1,739. Miss the promo deadline by a lot, though, and the gap shrinks fast. ### What credit score do I need for a 0% balance transfer? Most of the strong 0% offers go to applicants with scores of at least 670, in the good range or above. With fair credit, expect a decline, a shorter promo, or a limit too low to hold your full balance. ### What happens if I do not pay off the transfer in time? Whatever is left moves onto the card's standard APR, which can be close to 30%. You do not lose the interest you already saved on the part you paid off, but the leftover balance gets expensive quickly, so the plan only works if the payment is set high enough from month one. ### Can I transfer only part of my balance? Yes. Issuers set a transfer limit, and it may be lower than your total debt. If you can only move part of what you owe, move the balance with the highest interest rate first, so the most expensive debt stops growing. ### Will consolidating hurt my credit score? Applying puts a hard inquiry on your report and can dip your score for a while. After that, paying balances down lowers your credit utilization, which tends to help your score over time, as long as you do not run the cards back up. ## A quick disclaimer This article is general education, not financial advice. Rates, fees, and offers change often and vary by lender and country, so check current terms before you apply. If your debt feels unmanageable, a nonprofit credit counselor can review your full picture for free. ## Sources - [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, "What do I need to know about consolidating my credit card debt?"](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-do-i-need-to-know-if-im-thinking-about-consolidating-my-credit-card-debt-en-1861/) - [Experian, "What Is a Balance Transfer and Is It Worth It?" (March 2026).](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/what-is-a-balance-transfer-and-how-does-it-work/) - [Motley Fool Money, "The Average Credit Card Interest Rate" (reporting Federal Reserve data, updated July 2026).](https://www.fool.com/money/research/average-credit-card-interest-rate/)
